meta.tagline: La Rossa, La Dotta, La Grassa — the Red, the Learned, the Fat

overview.title: Welcome to Bologna
overview.intro: Bologna has three nicknames and every one earns its place. La Rossa — the red — for the terracotta rooftops and medieval brickwork that glow at golden hour. La Dotta — the learned — for the world's oldest university, founded in 1088, still filling every piazza with students and ideas. La Grassa — the fat — because Bologna invented tagliatelle al ragù, mortadella, tortellini, and tortelloni, and the Bolognese are entirely unapologetic about it. This is Italy's best-kept secret: a real city, with real food, real history, and almost no tourist crowds.

local_word.definition: The women who hand-roll pasta in Bologna — a centuries-old tradition. When a Bolognese says the sfoglina made the pasta, it means it's the real thing. The highest compliment a dish can receive. Look for it on menus and trust it completely.

rules.title: Bologna is a walking city — wear good shoes
rules.description: The historic center is compact, flat, and almost entirely walkable. The 40 km of UNESCO-listed porticoes keep you dry in rain and cool in sun. You will not need taxis or buses once you're in the center. Just walk — that's the entire point.

rules.title: Eat lunch — not dinner — as your main meal
rules.description: Bolognese culinary tradition centers on the midday meal. Restaurants are at their best, freshest, and most local at lunchtime. Many trattorias serve a Menu del Giorno — two or three courses, wine included, at remarkable value. This is how you eat here.

rules.title: Bolognese ragù is NOT what you think
rules.description: The real thing is slow-cooked, meat-heavy, with very little tomato — almost orange, not red. It is served with tagliatelle, never spaghetti. If a restaurant serves 'spaghetti bolognese' it is not a real Bolognese restaurant. Walk past it without looking back.

quick_facts.label: Airport
quick_facts.sub: Marconi Express · 7 min · direct to Centrale

quick_facts.label: Train hub
quick_facts.sub: Florence 35 min · Milan 1 hr · Rome 2 hr

tip.label: The secret acoustic wonder
tip.text: Under the Voltone del Podestà in Piazza Maggiore — stand in one corner, have a friend stand in the diagonally opposite corner, whisper into the wall. You'll hear each other perfectly. One of Bologna's Seven Secrets. Try it before you tell anyone.

transport.title: Getting Around
transport.intro: Bologna is Italy's most walkable city. Once you're in the historic center, you need almost no transport at all. Getting there from the airport is where the choices matter.

items.title: Airport (BLQ) → City Center
items.description: The Marconi Express monorail is the fastest — 7 minutes from the airport directly to Bologna Centrale station, departures every 15 minutes. From Centrale, the historic center is a 15-minute walk. The Aerobus shuttle is cheaper and drops you near Piazza Maggiore — good if your hotel is in the center. Taxis take about 20 minutes and are significantly more expensive.

items.title: Walking — your main transport
items.description: The entire historic center is about 2 km across. The 40 km of UNESCO-listed porticoes mean you can walk in any weather completely sheltered. From Bologna Centrale to Piazza Maggiore is a 15-minute walk. Almost everywhere you need to go is within 20 minutes on foot.

items.title: City Buses (TPER)
items.description: You'll rarely need a bus in the center, but they're useful for reaching San Luca basilica, Giardini Margherita park, or neighborhoods outside the walls. Buy tickets at tabacchi shops, machines at stops, or the Roger/Muver apps. Validate on board.

items.title: Cycling
items.description: Bologna is very cycle-friendly with dedicated lanes throughout the center. Rent bikes via BikeMi or Mobike apps, or from rental shops near the station. The flat terrain makes it easy and fast. Perfect for reaching neighborhoods like Bolognina or the university quarter.

items.title: Bologna as a base — day trips
items.description: Bologna Centrale is one of Italy's great rail hubs. Florence is 35 minutes by high-speed train, Milan 1 hour, Venice 1.5 hours, Rome 2 hours. Modena — home to the world's greatest balsamic vinegar and Ferrari museum — is just 17 minutes. One of the best bases in all of Italy.

callout.label: The San Luca pilgrimage
callout.text: To reach the Sanctuary of San Luca, walk the world's longest porticoed arcade — 3.8 km, 666 arches from Porta Saragozza. It takes 60–90 minutes uphill but the views and the achievement are worth every step. Or take the San Luca Express tourist train if you prefer.

stay.title: Where to Stay
stay.intro: Bologna's historic center is compact — almost everywhere inside the walls is a good choice. The differences are about atmosphere, not distance.

local_word.definition: A simple, traditional Italian eating and drinking place — more humble than a restaurant, more food-focused than a bar. Bologna's osterias are the real heart of the city's food culture. Finding yours in your neighbourhood is the first thing you do after checking in.

items.name: Centro Storico (Around Piazza Maggiore)
items.description: The absolute heart of Bologna. Medieval architecture, the Two Towers, the best trattorias, Piazza Maggiore itself. Walking distance to everything. Slightly noisier on weekend nights when students fill the piazzas, but nothing compared to the chaos of Rome or Florence.

items.name: Università Quarter
items.description: The area around Via Zamboni and the university buildings. Buzzing with student energy, independent bookshops, cheap aperitivo bars, street art. The oldest university in the world is still fully alive here — you feel 1088 and 2025 simultaneously. Great for younger travelers.

items.name: Quadrilatero & Santo Stefano
items.description: The old market district and the area around the beautiful Piazza Santo Stefano. Quieter than the main centro, incredibly atmospheric, surrounded by the best food shops, artisan workshops, and the hidden Osteria del Sole — the oldest pub in Bologna, open since 1465.

items.name: Bolognina (North of the Station)
items.description: Just north of Bologna Centrale, this working-class neighbourhood is rapidly becoming Bologna's most interesting. Multicultural food scene, local bars, street art, genuine neighbourhood life. 10-minute walk to the historic center. Where savvy travelers stay to save money without sacrificing anything.

best_time.title: Best Time to Visit
best_time.intro: Bologna is a city for every season — but each one offers something completely different. It's never overwhelmingly crowded, which is the whole point.

items.label: Spring
items.name: Perfect Weather
items.subtitle: Spring · Perfect Walking Weather
items.description: Mild temperatures, flowers in the piazzas, markets brimming with spring produce — artichokes, asparagus, peas. The university is fully alive, Piazza Maggiore hosts outdoor events and film screenings. Not yet crowded. This is when Bologna is at its most energetic and easiest to love.

callout.label: Don't miss
callout.text: Cineteca di Bologna outdoor cinema begins in spring — open-air film screenings in the piazza, free or very cheap. Unmissably Bolognese.

items.label: Summer
items.name: Hot & Local
items.subtitle: Summer · Hot, Quiet, Local
items.description: July and August see students leave and the city quieten. Temperatures can hit 35°C+ and humidity is high. But trattorias are less crowded, prices drop, and the city feels more genuinely local than any other time. The Sotto le Stelle del Cinema outdoor festival in Piazza Maggiore is magical.

callout.label: Heat warning
callout.text: August is genuinely hot. Many smaller restaurants close for 2–3 weeks in mid-August. Check ahead. The porticoes provide shade that makes midday walks bearable.

items.label: Autumn
items.name: Best Season
items.subtitle: Autumn · The Best Season
items.description: September to November is Bologna at its absolute peak. Students return, markets fill with truffles, porcini, and game, the light turns golden on the terracotta, and the food scene reaches its richest. October is white truffle season in nearby Alba — 45 minutes by train.

callout.label: Don't miss
callout.text: Mortadella BOlogna festival (September/October) — the entire city celebrates its most famous product. Free tastings, producers, events. The most Bologna thing that happens all year.

items.label: Winter
items.name: Cosy & Foggy
items.subtitle: Winter · Foggy, Cosy, Authentic
items.description: Bologna winters are foggy — the Po Valley fog (la nebbia) settles over the city and gives it a mysterious, cinematic atmosphere. The Christmas market in Piazza Maggiore is beautiful. Trattorias are warm and full of locals. The quietest, most affordable, and arguably most authentic time to visit.

callout.label: Insider tip
callout.text: January is the best month for osteria dining — locals only, no tourists, every place at its most authentic. The fog adds atmosphere that no other season can match.

monthly_highlights.text: Cinema Ritrovato + Sotto le Stelle: Piazza Maggiore becomes a giant open-air cinema, classic films screened for free.
Truffle season: Apennine white truffle lands on the menus; the Savigno truffle festival is worth a half-day escape.
Fiera di Santa Lucia: the centuries-old Christmas market under the Servi portico.
Arte Fiera + the quiet season: hotels are cheap, trattoria tables easy to find, and ragù tastes even better in winter.

eat.title: What to Eat
eat.intro: Bologna is Italy's undisputed food capital. Every dish here has a story, a tradition, and a Bolognese who will tell you you're eating it wrong.

local_word.definition: But in Bologna, the real greeting before a meal is 'Mangia bene!' — eat well. And in this city, that's not a wish. It's a guarantee.

items.name: Tagliatelle al Ragù — the real thing
items.description: NOT spaghetti bolognese. Tagliatelle — fresh, egg-based, hand-rolled — with a slow-cooked meat ragù that is almost orange, not red. The recipe is registered with the Bologna Chamber of Commerce. A restaurant without this dish doesn't understand Bologna.

items.name: Tortellini in Brodo
items.description: Tiny pasta parcels filled with pork loin, mortadella, prosciutto, Parmigiano-Reggiano, and nutmeg — served in clear capon broth. This is Bologna's soul in a bowl. Locals eat it on Christmas Eve. You should eat it the day you arrive.

items.name: Mortadella — not what you know
items.description: The original — IGP-protected, made only in Bologna, studded with pistachios and peppercorns, silky and sweet. Nothing like the processed version sold elsewhere. Get it thinly sliced at any salumeria in the Quadrilatero. Order a crescentina sandwich stuffed with it.

items.name: Parmigiano-Reggiano — taste the ages
items.description: You are 30 km from where this cheese is made. At any good salumeria, ask to taste 24-month, 36-month, and 48-month aged versions side by side. The difference is extraordinary. Buy a wedge to take home — significantly cheaper than anywhere else.
items.tag: Taste different ages side by side

items.name: Aperitivo Culture
items.description: Every evening 6–8 PM, Bologna's bars put out free food with every drink. Real food — pasta, bruschetta, meats, cheeses. Order a Spritz or Lambrusco (the local sparkling red wine), eat for free alongside it. This is the city's evening ritual.
items.tag: 6–8 PM · free food with every drink

items.name: Gelato — but properly
items.description: Look for gelato that is matte, not shiny, stored flat in metal pans with lids, not piled high in towers. Cremeria Funivia and Gelateria Gianni are the locals' choices. Never order from a place with neon-bright towers of gelato.
items.tag: Matte, not shiny · flat in pans

callout.label: The Quadrilatero ritual
callout.text: Bologna's ancient market district — a grid of medieval streets between Piazza Maggiore and the Two Towers. Go in the morning. Buy mortadella at one stall, Parmigiano at another, a glass of Pignoletto wine at the counter. Eat standing up. This is exactly how Bolognese have done it for centuries.

hidden_gems.title: Hidden Gems
hidden_gems.intro: Bologna rewards the curious like few cities in Italy. The best things here are behind unmarked doors, up medieval towers, and through tiny windows.

items.name: Finestrella di Via Piella
items.description: A tiny window cut into a wall on Via Piella — look through it and see one of Bologna's secret canals, reflecting the medieval buildings above. Called La Piccola Venezia (Little Venice). Go early morning or late evening for the best light. Walk 20 meters further for a second canal view through a grate in the street.

items.name: Osteria del Sole — no sign on the door
items.description: Open since 1465, hidden in the Quadrilatero with no sign outside. Inside: low ceilings, long shared wooden tables, locals drinking wine at noon. No food served — bring your own from the market stalls outside. Order a glass of house wine at the counter. One of the most genuine places in Italy.

items.name: Santo Stefano — the Seven Churches
items.description: From the outside: one bulky medieval building. Inside: a complex of seven interconnected churches from different centuries. Dating back to the 5th century. One of Bologna's most extraordinary and most overlooked monuments. Almost no queue, almost no tourists. Free entry.

items.name: Archiginnasio Anatomical Theatre
items.description: Inside the Archiginnasio — once the main building of the world's oldest university — a fully intact 17th-century anatomical theatre carved entirely from wood, where early medical students watched dissections by candlelight. One of the most extraordinary rooms in Italy. Small entry fee. Almost always crowd-free.

items.name: Biblioteca Salaborsa — glass floor to ancient Rome
items.description: The public library next to Piazza Maggiore has a transparent glass floor — look down through it at the excavated ruins of Roman roads and buildings. Free to enter. Almost no tourist knows it's there. Go, look down, say nothing.

items.name: The Fountain of Neptune — one specific angle
items.description: From a very specific angle — directly from the southwest corner — the thumb of Neptune's outstretched hand creates a suggestive optical illusion that sculptor Giambologna deliberately hid from the censors in 1566. Find the angle. You'll know it immediately.

callout.label: The porticoed pilgrimage
callout.text: The walk to the Sanctuary of San Luca — 3.8 km uphill through the world's longest porticoed arcade, 666 arches, from Porta Saragozza. Leave early morning. The city spreads below you at the top. Bologna's best-kept experience.

items.label: Eat tagliatelle al ragù at a real trattoria
items.sub: With tagliatelle — never spaghetti. Ask if the sfoglina made the pasta.

items.label: Find the Finestrella di Via Piella
items.sub: The little window to Little Venice. Go at golden hour.

items.label: Try the acoustic whisper trick in Piazza Maggiore
items.sub: Voltone del Podestà — opposite corners, whisper into the wall.

items.label: Visit the Anatomical Theatre in the Archiginnasio
items.sub: Small entry fee, no queue, one of the most extraordinary rooms in Italy.

items.label: Drink wine at Osteria del Sole
items.sub: No sign on the door. Bring your own food from the market. Since 1465.

items.label: Walk through the Quadrilatero in the morning
items.sub: Buy mortadella, Parmigiano, a glass of Pignoletto. Eat standing up.

items.label: Look through the glass floor at Biblioteca Salaborsa
items.sub: Ancient Rome under the library. Free. Almost no one knows.

items.label: Have aperitivo with free food at a local bar
items.sub: 6–8 PM. Order a Lambrusco. Eat the free spread. This is Bologna evenings.

items.label: Walk the porticoed path to San Luca
items.sub: 3.8 km, 666 arches, world's longest porticoed arcade. Views at the top.

items.label: Eat tortellini in brodo
items.sub: Bologna's soul in a bowl. Especially good in winter.

items.label: Find Neptune's hidden optical illusion
items.sub: Southwest corner of the fountain. The thumb. You'll understand immediately.

traps.title: Skip the Traps
traps.intro: Bologna is one of Italy's least touristy big cities; the traps are few, but they exist. Know them, and save your stomach for the real Bologna.

items.name: Anywhere with 'Spaghetti Bolognese' on the menu
items.description: No such dish exists in Bologna; ragù is served with tagliatelle. A menu advertising 'spag bol' is an announcement: we cook for tourists.
items.instead: Look for 'tagliatelle al ragù'; the trattorias rolling their sfoglia by hand are obvious from the doorway.

items.name: Tables right on Piazza Maggiore
items.description: Cafés facing the square charge two or three times more, coperto included. The view is lovely, but the same espresso costs a third two streets back.
items.instead: Drink standing up on the square; to sit and eat, slip into the Quadrilatero's side streets or Via del Pratello.

items.name: Souvenir 'balsamic vinegar' bottles
items.description: Most shiny bottles in tourist shops are caramelised grape juice. Real Aceto Balsamico Tradizionale di Modena ages at least 12 years and is sold sealed.
items.instead: Look for the DOP seal; buy from a trusted salumeria and taste before you pay.

items.name: Mistaking FICO for 'real Bologna food'
items.description: The giant food park outside town can be fun, but Bologna's food soul isn't there; the miracle is in the century-old shops of the centre.
items.instead: Spend that half day in the Quadrilatero instead: Mercato di Mezzo, the salumerias, the cheese shops — all within a short walk.

callout.label: The golden rule
callout.text: In Bologna the mark of a good place is a handwritten menu and few tables. The shorter the menu, the prouder the kitchen.

itinerary.title: Ready-Made Routes
itinerary.intro: If you hate planning, follow these flows. The times are flexible; keep the spirit, break the order.

plans.title: If You Have 1 Day
plans.subtitle: Porticoes, towers and the pasta of your life

steps.title: Piazza Maggiore + San Petronio
steps.description: An espresso standing at the corner of the square, then into San Petronio with its famously unfinished façade.

steps.title: Quadrilatero wander
steps.description: Medieval market lanes: salumeria windows, the scent of mortadella, Mercato di Mezzo. Save room for lunch.

steps.title: Tagliatelle al ragù
steps.description: Eat the pasta of your life at a trattoria. Lunch is the main event; that is how Bologna works.

steps.title: Santo Stefano + Finestrella
steps.description: Explore the seven-church complex, then peek through the little window on Via Piella at the hidden canal.

steps.title: Asinelli Tower or San Luca
steps.description: 498 steps for the rooftop view; or walk under the porticoes toward San Luca instead.

steps.title: Evening on Via del Pratello
steps.description: Aperitivo on the students' and locals' street, then an osteria. At Osteria del Sole: wine, plus the salumi you brought yourself.

plans.title: If You Have 3 Days
plans.subtitle: Live the city as a guest, not a tourist

steps.title: The centre and the classics
steps.description: The 1-day flow above: Maggiore, Quadrilatero, ragù, the towers.

steps.title: University and hidden corners
steps.description: The anatomical theatre of the Archiginnasio, Via Zamboni, Salaborsa's glass floor. Gelato on Piazza Santo Stefano in the afternoon, tortellini in brodo at night.

steps.title: San Luca and a slow goodbye
steps.description: Walk to the Madonna di San Luca under 666 arches of portico (3.8 km, all covered). One last crescentina on the way back; the station is five minutes away.

phrases.title: The 5-Word Survival Kit
phrases.intro: A few words of Italian open every door; in Bologna they open stomachs too.

items.meaning: Hi / bye — any hour, to anyone
Thanks a lot — never overkill, always works
Please — add it to the end of your order
Cheers! — glasses rise with Lambrusco here
How delicious! — the sentence you'll need most in Bologna
